newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico ruling party closes ranks behind Zedillo.
newsitem.headline: Mexico ruling party closes ranks behind Zedillo.

text.p: After earlier attacking government free-market policies, Mexico's ruling party ended a key assembly on Sunday by closing ranks behind President Ernesto Zedillo and his drive for a more democratic, open society.
Delegates had spent Saturday railing against the PRI's "technocrats" -- foreign-educated administrators whom they blame for economic crisis, political corruption and waning electoral support.

Against the wishes of the pro-Zedillo party leadership, militants rewrote PRI rules to oppose the privatisation of the petrochemical industry. They also insisted that future candidates for president of the republic must have held elected office and been party members for 10 years -- rules that would have disqualified Zedillo had they been in place when he ran.

But in the time-honoured fashion of a party that has ruled for 67 unbroken years, delegates closed ranks at Sunday's closing plenary, cheering enthusiastically as they heard a speech from the PRI's best-known technocrat -- the Yale-educated former central banker Zedillo.

In another move to sweep controversy under the carpet, the PRI also decided not to take any decision about expelling one of its least popular former members, ex-president Carlos Salinas, who is blamed for triggering economic crisis and tolerating massive corruption.
The party chose instead to refer the matter of Salinas's party membership to its Honour and Justice Committee -- the same group that decided last year not to expel him.

Zedillo, who has made much of his wish to distance himself from the PRI, returned the assembly's compliments to him Sunday by declaring his "great pride" in what he termed "the party of my convictions, the party of my political militancy."

"I reject that the respect I have had and will continue to have invariably for the (party) processes and decisions ... is maliciously confused with indifference ... or still worse, with disagreement or a rupture," Zedillo said.

In keeping with Sunday's tone of unity, party secretary-general Juan Millan changed the agenda to avoid reading the modifications made by militants Saturday to party statutes and principles. Instead, he asked for block approval from the 4,423 delegates of all the changes as a whole.
Texts were not available, but Millan assured the assembly that leaders of the party's key sectors had read and approved them previously as representing the party's will.

Presidential officials were already attempting to put their spin on the assembly's more radical decisions, such as voting in the early hours of Sunday morning that all PRI members holding government office -- including presumably Zedillo -- must donate 5 percent of their salary to party funds.

"I don't think this assembly necessarily changes anything," one official said. "You must remember that the president was elected by the people of Mexico in 1994 to carry out a programme and he will continue to carry that programme out. He is not necessarily bound by decisions made here."

One of the more uncomfortable decisions for ministers was a unanimous vote Saturday in a workshop considering party principles to declare all-out opposition to the privatisation of the petrochemical industry -- a major policy plank of the Zedillo government, albeit one that was already facing strong opposition in Congress.

Poltical commentators said the major significance of the assembly was the chance Saturday's debates gave rank-and-file PRI members to speak their mind. Previous assemblies were generally sewn up well in advance, with no controversial debate allowed.
During a session Saturday covering party statutes, delegates roared, clenched their fists and bellowed demands that the party return to its socialist roots in the 1910-17 Mexican Revolution.
Since 1982, three successive PRI presidents of Mexico have broken with the party's left-wing, nationalistic past to encourage free markets and foreign investment.
